title: Iterative Label Refinement Matters More than Preference Optimization under Weak Supervision

contributions.purpose: Determine whether the standard SFT+RLHF post-training pipeline remains effective when human supervision is unreliable (as it becomes for hard-to-supervise tasks), and diagnose why DPO fails.
contributions.mechanism: Analysis via a controlled simulation of unreliable supervision using small LMs (a weak generator p-tilde for demonstrations, a weak classifier q-tilde for comparisons) and, separately, time-constrained human annotators; measure SFT vs SFT+DPO and vary the DPO KL-regularization coefficient beta across feedback-quality levels to isolate the overoptimization mechanism.
contributions.evaluation: On GSM8K, BIRD, SaferPaca with weak-to-strong setups (2B->7B, 7B->70B, 2B->70B): SFT beats the weak supervisor (W2SG) but DPO gives little/no gain over SFT under unreliable feedback; with oracle feedback DPO does improve. Overoptimization shown: small beta helps with oracle feedback but hurts with unreliable feedback, while large beta (needed to curb overoptimization) blocks the large updates required to fix SFT errors.
contributions.domain: LLM post-training / alignment (RLHF) under unreliable supervision
contributions.source_quote: We find that in the presence of unreliable supervision, SFT still retains some effectiveness, but DPO (a common RLHF algorithm) fails to improve the model beyond SFT.

contributions.purpose: Provide an alternative to RLHF that better uses comparison feedback under unreliable supervision, avoiding DPO's regularization dilemma while still allowing large model updates.
contributions.mechanism: Iterative Label Refinement (ILR): each round splits the SFT data in half, trains two SFT models that cross-label the held-out half to propose alternative demonstrations, uses comparison feedback (weak LM or humans) to decide whether each model proposal replaces the original label (updating at most alpha|X| labels by confidence, alpha=0.15), then retrains a fresh SFT model from the base PLM on the refined dataset; repeated for K rounds.
contributions.evaluation: Qualitative mechanism plus quantitative gains (see C3); ILR yields much larger KL divergence from the initial SFT model than DPO after one round and improves SFT-label accuracy round over round (Fig 5), approaching/surpassing ground-truth-trained model accuracy when feedback is reliable.
contributions.source_quote: ILR improves the SFT data by using comparison feedback to decide whether human demonstrations should be replaced by model-generated alternatives, then retrains the model via SFT on the updated data.

contributions.purpose: Show SFT+ILR outperforms SFT+DPO under unreliable supervision across diverse tasks and under real (time-constrained) human feedback.
contributions.mechanism: Head-to-head comparison of SFT+ILR vs SFT+DPO over multiple rounds in four LM-simulated settings and a CloudResearch human study on Alpaca (1000 demonstrations at 1-2 min each, 1000 comparisons/round at 30-60s each, 2 rounds).
contributions.evaluation: SFT+ILR consistently beats SFT+DPO on GSM8K (2B->7B and 7B->70B), BIRD (2B->70B), and SaferPaca (2B->7B win rate); in the human study ILR improves fast and consistently while DPO with small beta plateaus and large beta improves slowly; ILR benefits from scale (larger gains at 70B).
contributions.source_quote: SFT+ILR outperforms SFT+DPO on several tasks with unreliable supervision (math, coding, and safe instruction-following).

self_declared_provenance.quote: The SFT stage in our LM-based simulation employs a similar setting as the setup used for studying W2SG in Burns et al. (2023) but extended to text generation tasks; Burns et al. (2023) only consider classification tasks.

Our cross-labeling framework shares conceptual similarities with co-training (Blum & Mitchell, 1998; Zhou et al., 2005) and co-teaching (Han et al., 2018), although these methods primarily focus on classification settings and rely on model confidence scores.

Recent work has also investigated the impact of noisy preference data on RLHF (Chowdhury et al., 2024; Fisch et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2024), while our work addresses a more challenging case where both SFT data and preference data are unreliable.

notes: Central result is a NEGATIVE result about the standard pipeline: DPO/RLHF fails to improve over SFT under unreliable supervision (overoptimization + regularization dilemma), challenging RLHF as the best use of human feedback. Additional negative finding: naively replacing labels with model proposals WITHOUT comparison feedback degrades performance (model collapse from uncurated synthetic data), so supervision in refinement is necessary. Caveat/trade-off: ILR's benefit decreases over rounds in the human study (annotators pick fewer AI outputs later; W2SG may be insufficient). Limitations acknowledged: only DPO studied (not PPO/reward modeling); time-constrained humans may not capture real capability limits; tasks are not truly beyond human ability.
